podcast.title: Discovery and Recording Debut (1929)
podcast.body: In 1929, Memphis Mini was discovered by someone from Columbia Records while she was performing outside a barbershop. This led to her traveling to New York, where she recorded her first blues songs with her second husband, Joe McCoy. "In 1929, she was discovered by someone from Columbia Records while playing outside of Barber Shop."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Retirement and Death (1950s-1973)
podcast.body: Memphis Mini's health declined in the 1950s, forcing her to retire from music. A series of strokes eventually destroyed her ability to play the guitar, and she passed away in a nursing home in 1973. "For the decades, she would record many more songs, but declining health in the 1950s forced her to retire."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Headstone Memorial (1996)
podcast.body: In 1996, Bonnie Wright funded a headstone for Memphis Mini, which features an inscription acknowledging her profound contribution to the blues. The inscription highlights how her hundreds of recorded sides serve as essential material for understanding the genre, speaking for millions through a singular, individual voice that reflects personal fantasies, dreams, and desires. "The hundreds of sides Mini recorded are the perfect material to teach us about the blues."

podcast.title: Discovery and Early Career
podcast.body: In 1929, she was discovered by a representative from Columbia Records while performing outside a barbershop, leading to a trip to New York where she recorded blues songs with her second husband, Joe McCoy. By 1935, Memphis Minnie had become an established artist, recognized as one of the very few female blues guitarists. "In 1929, she was discovered by someone from Columbia Records while playing outside of Barber Shop."

podcast.title: Early Life and Tough Demeanor
podcast.body: Born Lizzie Douglas in Louisiana in 1897, she ran away from home at 13 to play guitar on the streets of Memphis and reportedly worked as a prostitute when necessary. Known for her toughness, she was unafraid to fight, even resorting to a knife or pistol if a situation became confrontational. "She was tough. If things got heavy, she wasn't afraid to fight, whether she needed to pull a knife or a pistol."

podcast.title: Early Life and Tough Demeanor
podcast.body: Born Lizzie Douglas in Louisiana in 1897, Memphis Mini ran away from home at the age of 13 to play guitar on the street corners of Memphis. When busking didn't provide enough income, she reportedly worked as a prostitute, and she was known for her toughness, unafraid to fight and capable of using a knife or pistol if necessary. "She was tough. If things got heavy, she wasn't afraid to fight, whether she needed to pull a knife or a pistol."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Pioneering Female Blues Guitarist
podcast.body: By 1935, Memphis Mini had established herself as an artist, becoming one of the very few female blues guitarists of her time. Over the decades, she recorded numerous songs, showcasing her unique talent in a male-dominated field. "By 1935, Memphis Mini was an established artist, one of the very few female blues guitarists."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Retirement and Posthumous Recognition
podcast.body: After decades of recording numerous songs, her declining health in the 1950s, including a series of strokes that impaired her ability to play guitar, forced her to retire. She passed away in a nursing home in 1973, but in 1996, Bonnie Raitt funded a headstone for her, inscribed with an epitaph praising her singular contribution to the blues. "A series of strokes destroyed her ability to play guitar, and she died in a nursing home in 1973."
